item.title: Elon Musk joins 165,000 others calling for Nvidia to bring back Jensen Huang in open letter
item.description: CEO ousted after affair with suspected Chinese spy reportedly plans comeback, as US treasury secretary urges ‘dramatic shake-up’ Megaspeed says it’s a ‘legitimate and lawful business’ Business live – latest updates Elon Musk and a host of other tech bosses have called for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia, amid reports the former chief executive is already plotting a return to the chip company just four days after his resignation. An open letter, which has more than 165,000 signatories, demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”. Continue reading...

item.title: Senator slams Commerce Secretary for flow of Nvidia AI chips to China
item.description: Washington Senator Maria Cantwell, one of the top Democrats on the Senate commerce committee, has taken fire at the Department of Commerce (DOC) under Secretary Howard Lutnick for neglecting to enforce protections intended to keep Nvidia's AI chips away from China. In a letter to Lutnick on Sunday, Cantwell said the DOC has "undermined America's national security," and that its failures "help give away America's technology advantage in AI." "Despite clear authority from Congress, the Department of Commerce has allowed advanced AI chips to flow through companies with ties to the People's Republic of China (PRC). The Department of Commerce h … Read the full story at The Verge.

item.title: Omaxian takes the Omarchy look down a different Linux backstreet
item.description: Omaxian OS is only at version 0.1, but it already takes a distinctly unconventional route through the Linux desktop. The brand-new Linux desktop distro describes itself as "the Omarchy desktop on X11 — as a shell for your Debian, or as a whole OS." That's not quite the impression that we came away with, though. Like most distros, Omaxian is available as an ISO file you can install and use. Alternatively, Omaxian Shell can be installed on an existing Debian-family distro without replacing the underlying operating system. The OS release is codenamed "Trans-Siberian Shaman," and the GitHub project repository shows work going back just a few weeks. No LLM coding assistant is credited on the project page, but we looked inside some of the test scripts, and as well as being verbose and hard to read, they also credit "Grok Bot." Omarchy itself is of course built with LLM assistance, and as we reported last month , so is the new Daemonarchy FreeBSD-based desktop project. Omaxian is styled after Omarchy, and it includes some of the same tools – and optional support for LLMs – but it's not based on the same tech. Instead of Arch, it's based on Devuan 6, the current version of the systemd-free fork of Debian. Omaxian eschews Hyprland, and indeed Wayland altogether: it opts for an X11 tiling window manager – in this case, i3 . i3 first appeared in 2009, so it's been around much longer than Hyprland. Omaxian's configuration also understands familiar keystrokes such as Alt+F4 to close a window. For us, that's a significant usability win. The window manager isn't running on top of X.org. Omaxian uses the 2025 fork, the new XLibre X11 server . This is a controversial project led by a controversial developer , which will be enough for some people to want to avoid Omaxian as a whole. The latest release of GhostBSD uses XLibre too, though. Way back in 2021, The Register reported on Omarchy creator David Heinemeier Hansson's company banning political discussions, and things have only got more vexed since. Just as DHH has attracted some notoriety for his now right-wing views, his Linux is similarly opinionated. If the associations surrounding Omarchy and XLibre put you off, Omaxian's combination of the two probably won't win you over. The flipside is that if you don't care about the political views, but are interested in the idea of a tiling environment set up for power users who embrace LLM coding assistance, then you might like Omaxian. The full distro trades Arch, Wayland, and systemd for a Devuan base, X11, and sysvinit, with APT handling conventional packages. Flatpaks and AppImages are available too. We tried Omaxian in VirtualBox, but we experienced frequent display corruption. We must give it this: the interface is slightly easier to navigate than Hyprland. One touch that we did like is that if you get tired of the tiling stuff and want to switch back to something more conventional, then Xfce is also installed in the background. The brand-new Linux desktop distro describes itself as "the Omarchy desktop on X11 — as a shell for your Debian, or as a whole OS." That's not quite the impression that we came away with, though. Omaxian uses the 2025 fork, the new XLibre X11 server . This is a controversial project led by a controversial developer , which will be enough for some people to want to avoid Omaxian as a whole. The latest release of GhostBSD uses XLibre too, though. Way back in 2021, The Register reported on Omarchy creator David Heinemeier Hansson's company banning political discussions, and things have only got more vexed since. Just as DHH has attracted some notoriety for his now right-wing views, his Linux is similarly opinionated. If the associations surrounding Omarchy and XLibre put you off, Omaxian's combination of the two probably won't win you over. The flipside is that if you don't care about the political views, but are interested in the idea of a tiling environment set up for power users who embrace LLM coding assistance, then you might like Omaxian. One touch that we did like is that if you get tired of the tiling stuff and want to switch back to something more conventional, then Xfce is also installed in the background. Xfce provides Omaxian with a file manager and other accessories, but you can just choose Xfce from the login screen and find yourself back in a simple, familiar, classic desktop environment. Omaxian is not the sort of environment we're looking for. This vulture isn't a developer and doesn't use LLMs for anything at all. However, lots of people are looking for something like that, as demonstrated by Omarchy's sponsorship . But it's bold, colorful, and significantly different from the mainstream, and that is the sort of thing we do like to see. ®

item.title: Albanese treads tightrope in upcoming Trump meeting, wanting Indo-Pacific engagement and end to Iran and Ukraine wars
item.description: Quad leaders’ summit in Philippines is Trump’s first, as Australia joins US and Japan to protect AI technologies in face of China efforts to dominate Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast Anthony Albanese will attempt to walk a tightrope in his relationship with Donald Trump when the pair meets on Tuesday, arguing for a speedy resolution to the wars in Iran and Ukraine while urging the US to engage in the Indo-Pacific. The Quad leaders’ summit in the Philippines’ capital of Manila will be Trump’s first, in either of his presidencies. The US president, fresh from a crushing midterms result, will take centre stage in gatherings of Asian leaders and prepare for historic three-way talks with Xi Jinping of China and Russia’s Vladimir Putin this week. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here Continue reading...

item.title: We don't need no education platform evolution. Hey, Redmond, leave those kids alone
item.description: "Give me the child until he is seven, and I will give you the man." This saying about the importance of influence in early education is variously attributed either to St Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Jesuits, or Aristotle, depending on whether you wanted to entrust your very young son to Catholic priests or ancient Greeks. Fortunately for both groups, perhaps, neither of them ever said that, even though both certainly believed it. Another group that certainly believes it is the cadre of tech company policy makers, which goes a long way to explain the cultural and legislative backlash to what happens to young people online. The least pernicious and longest established example of the catch 'em young principle is the educational discount for hardware and software. Apple has been the highest profile company to do this, with hardware discounts and aggressively positioned complete service packages for educational institutions, often integrated with funding authorities. If you grow up using a package or platform, it becomes your first tech language and you're likely to become a lifetime customer. Microsoft has also played this long game, seasoned where it can with curriculum integration. Its latest wheeze, described by the company as educational platform evolution is a response to institutions' changing needs, with clearer pathways to adopting and enabling new technologies. Yada, as we say, yada. The evolved platform removes email and Teams from the free student tier, while imposing the requirement for Windows hardware to qualify, along with comprehensive restructuring of higher tiers and storage not necessarily to the advantage of the educators. This is the same sort of evolution to evolving needs as the British Empire brought to natives of other lands. Hello, India. Greetings, Africa. Whassup, America! These warships packed with gun-toting Brits are here to evolve your changing needs in local resource management. Microsoft has realized what Imperial Great Britain adopted as its primary principle. If you can get your future, ahem, customers over a barrel, then not only can you imprint your brand on their minds, you can take their money. You have to come up with some balderdash to cover it, whether it's about civilization and progress or enabling educators to… oh God, these poor fingers can't even type this stuff. Missing completely is the idea that educators' evolving needs may not include spending even more money on basic necessary services when budgets are stretched tight. Moreover, while existing uses of the old tier can stay on it until the end of next year, new sign-ups have to be on the Enhanced Speedy plans. Keen students of history, especially those in the former colonial lands of Eastern North America, may care to refresh their memories of events some 250 years ago. It is quite natural, when being bent over a barrel ceases to be an amusing pastime, to seek a less barrel-shaped position. In this case, the pressure to find alternatives has
item.dc:creator: Rupert Goodwins
item.content:encoded: "Give me the child until he is seven, and I will give you the man." This saying about the importance of influence in early education is variously attributed either to St Ignatius of Loyola, founder of the Jesuits, or Aristotle, depending on whether you wanted to entrust your very young son to Catholic priests or ancient Greeks. Fortunately for both groups, perhaps, neither of them ever said that, even though both certainly believed it. Another group that certainly believes it is the cadre of tech company policy makers, which goes a long way to explain the cultural and legislative backlash to what happens to young people online. The least pernicious and longest established example of the catch 'em young principle is the educational discount for hardware and software. Apple has been the highest profile company to do this, with hardware discounts and aggressively positioned complete service packages for educational institutions, often integrated with funding authorities. If you grow up using a package or platform, it becomes your first tech language and you're likely to become a lifetime customer. Microsoft has also played this long game, seasoned where it can with curriculum integration. Its latest wheeze, described by the company as educational platform evolution is a response to institutions' changing needs, with clearer pathways to adopting and enabling new technologies. Yada, as we say, yada. The evolved platform removes email and Teams from the free student tier, while imposing the requirement for Windows hardware to qualify, along with comprehensive restructuring of higher tiers and storage not necessarily to the advantage of the educators. This is the same sort of evolution to evolving needs as the British Empire brought to natives of other lands. Hello, India. Greetings, Africa. Whassup, America! These warships packed with gun-toting Brits are here to evolve your changing needs in local resource management. Microsoft has realized what Imperial Great Britain adopted as its primary principle. If you can get your future, ahem, customers over a barrel, then not only can you imprint your brand on their minds, you can take their money. You have to come up with some balderdash to cover it, whether it's about civilization and progress or enabling educators to… oh God, these poor fingers can't even type this stuff. Missing completely is the idea that educators' evolving needs may not include spending even more money on basic necessary services when budgets are stretched tight. Moreover, while existing uses of the old tier can stay on it until the end of next year, new sign-ups have to be on the Enhanced Speedy plans. Keen students of history, especially those in the former colonial lands of Eastern North America, may care to refresh their memories of events some 250 years ago. It is quite natural, when being bent over a barrel ceases to be an amusing pastime, to seek a less barrel-shaped position. In this case, the pressure to find alternatives has many elements. As well as the cost, support for Macs and Chromebooks becomes problematic. Both platforms are heavily represented in education at various levels, with the Macbook Neo thundering onto the battlefield with colors flying. Add to that the pressure towards digital sovereignty in Microsoft's own colonial outposts, the accelerants for an Old World version of the Boston Tea Party are only building. We even have a Boston of our very own . It's very nice. Microsoft isn't threatening anyone with guns and rapine, not yet anyway, and the whipping away of free student access to email and Teams only feels like extortion because of the misery it is causing across the sector. It is perfectly legal for Microsoft to cause as much suffering coated in balderdash as it likes. It is also perfectly legal to return the favor by actively seeking a sector-wide migration strategy. There are pioneers to learn from, especially huge multi-state, multi-supply chain organizations like Airbus and the various European governmental entities that are some way down that path already. This growing pool of expertise may be the most important factor in being able to react to Microsoft's efforts to turn education into a science fair experiment in high velocity frog boiling — one where the frog most definitely feels the heat — that and the growing distaste for the antics of American big tech. It's not just the forcing of unwanted technology that makes the barrel increasingly unbearable, nor using that as an excuse to charge more, it's what the companies are actually trying to do in Europe. Google Chromebooks are nice. Google wolves invading your villages because the company illegally erased their ecosystem are not nice. You thought those Wi-Fi snooping Maps cars were bad? The Microsoft educational platform "evolution" is foolhardy, counterproductive, and hugely tone deaf. It will not make it new lifetime customers, it will increase the speed at which its already hostile constituency grows resentment and appetite for radical action. Colonies revolt when the time is right, and empires are lost when arrogance and under-estimation of the situation combine with mismanagement and strategic blindness. The US midterms showed how that storm is blowing in. To choose this time to provoke an entire global sector is functional illiteracy writ large. Perhaps Microsoft should get an education. ®

item.title: Apple MacBook Pro M6 review: probably the last of its generation
item.description: Spec bump adds power to exceptionally long battery life in base-model Pro laptop, but is overshadowed by a new design Apple’s base-model MacBook Pro gets a solid speed bump, offering most of the features from its top-level siblings but in a design that has just been superseded and may soon be phased out. It is the starting model in Apple’s popular MacBook Pro line, but that doesn’t make it cheap. Costing from £1,999 (€2,299/$1,999/A$3,199) it is £300 or equivalent more than its predecessor as RAMageddon continues to jack up prices. It is, at least, £500 cheaper than the other new MacBook Pros. Screen: 14.2in mini LED (3024x1964; 254 ppi) ProMotion (120Hz) Processor: Apple M6 RAM: 16, 24 or 32GB Storage: 1, 2 or 4TB SSD Operating system: macOS 26.4 Tahoe Camera: 12MP Centre Stage Connectivity: wifi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, 3x Thunderbolt 4/USB 4, HDMI 2.1, SDXC, headphones Dimensions: 221.2 x 312.6 x 15.5mm Weight: 1.55kg Continue reading...

item.title: Techie rigged off-spec fan near flammable liquid and an exposed motherboard, then left it to run for days
item.description: If you've made mistakes at work that threatened to torch your career, The Register has just the column for you. We call it Who, Me? , we print one every Monday, and you're reading this week's instalment! Today, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Axl" who once worked at a petrol station (aka a gas station for US readers). One Friday afternoon, in the shadow of a holiday weekend, the PC that drove the station's pumps and point of sale stopped working, leaving it unable to operate. Axl called the manufacturer and got the very unwelcome news that a technician could visit on Tuesday at the earliest. As the petrol station was in a spot that would attract a few weekend tourists, the potential losses were substantial, and Axl felt he needed to act. He knew the main computer lived inside a large metal box affixed to a wall, an arrangement that meant electronics and flammable vapors were always kept well apart. The machine's power switch was accessible, so Axl turned it off and on again – and watched the machine come back to life, before shutting itself down five minutes later. That behavior was a strong hint that something was overheating but confirming that theory was not easy because the metal case included a lock (see previous remarks about preventing fires) and Axl didn't have they key. Axl inspected the hinges on the box, found they were held on with screws and was able to remove the lid and access the PC. "Aside from the considerable amount of dust and hair inside, I could see that the CPU fan was not turning," he wrote. "Either it had failed or was not receiving the control signal to cool." The service station had an office out the back. Axl liberated a desk fan, pointed it at the PC, and watched it come alive again. An hour later, the PC was still working, so Axl decided he needed a fix that would last the weekend. "I drove to a local electrical shop and purchased a high speed bathroom extraction fan which I rigged up inside the case, then closed it up best I could with tape and cardboard," he told The Register . That rickety rig kept fuel flowing for three days. "On Tuesday afternoon, the support engineer arrived and I explained how I kept us in business over the weekend," Axl wrote. "He just shrugged his shoulders, smiled and changed the failed fan. I didn't even get the 'It's our kit, leave it alone' lecture." He did get the satisfaction of a job well done. "No one died from an exploding petrol station and the tourists were happy they could go home," he wrote. Have you made a risky fix in a dangerous place? If so, the safe option is to click here and send your story to Who, Me? We promise to handle it with care and hopefully share it on some future Monday. ®

item.title: UK exposed to polycrisis of threats amid government ‘complacency’
item.description: Lords report calls for urgent new approach to resilience planning in face of cyber-attacks, sabotage and climate crisis Ministers are complacent in the face of fast-changing and increasingly interconnected threats to the UK, and must act quickly to increase national resilience to possibly very major crises, a parliamentary report has found. While Labour recently launched a “Be Ready” campaign, advising households to have stocks of food and water, most of the public are unaware of the scale of potential threats from cyber-attacks, proxy acts of violence or strikes on underseas cables, as well as natural disasters such as extreme weather and flooding, it said. Continue reading...

item.title: Microsoft’s Azure Linux dons Fedora to dress itself up for mainstream workloads
item.description: Microsoft has issued version 4.0 of its very own Azure Linux, which it built atop Fedora for the first time and now suggests is ready to run mainstream workloads. Redmond’s history with Linux is long and tangled. Former CEO Steve Ballmer infamously labelled the project a cancer but by 2015 Microsoft had quietly adapted the OS to power some switches in its Azure Cloud. Microsoft then built some of its own Azure services on containers and created a lightweight Linux for them to run in. In 2020, Microsoft released that Linux as CBL-Mariner, largely so that developers who used services like Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) that relied on the OS could access the platform they were building for. In 2022, CBL-Mariner became Azure Linux 2.0, another container-centric lightweight release. Version 3.0 followed in 2024, now billed as ready for “broad Azure usage” with Azure Kubernetes Service. In June 2026, Microsoft announced version 4.0 and billed it as suitable for Azure Virtual Machines, VM Scale Sets, and container images. The big change that made that repositioning possible was basing the OS on Fedora rather than Microsoft’s own Common Base Linux. Microsoft also tuned the Linux kernel – version 6.18 LTS – by adding Hyper-V guest drivers and other features that make it behave well in Azure. It also natively supports tools like Microsoft Defender for Cloud, Azure Monitor, and the Azure CLI, which Microsoft reckons committed Azure users already employ and therefore want to apply to their cloudy Linux workloads. Or as Redmond puts it: “the familiarity of [the] RPM package ecosystem, while adding Azure-native security, compliance, and operational capabilities.” All of those changes add up to an OS that Microsoft says is worth a look “Whether you're running web applications, databases, or GPU-accelerated AI/ML workloads.” Redmond makes that recommendation in part because Azure Linux comes with “no additional OS licensing cost.” Other commercial Linux distributions will cost users money, meaning Microsoft can now make an argument that SUSE and RHEL subscriptions might be superfluous for both AKS users and those who use Azure to host other applications on Linux. Azure Linux 4.0 debuted last Thursday and is available here . Redmond’s latest Linux debuted just days after Microsoft issued a monster upgrade to version 3.0. ®

Or as Redmond puts it: “the familiarity of [the] RPM package ecosystem, while adding Azure-native security, compliance, and operational capabilities.” All of those changes add up to an OS that Microsoft says is worth a look “Whether you're running web applications, databases, or GPU-accelerated AI/ML workloads.” Redmond makes that recommendation in part because Azure Linux comes with “no additional OS licensing cost.” Other commercial Linux distributions will cost users money, meaning Microsoft can now make an argument that SUSE and RHEL subscriptions might be superfluous for both AKS users and those who use Azure to host other applications on Linux. Azure Linux 4.0 debuted last Thursday and is available here . Redmond’s latest Linux debuted just days after Microsoft issued a monster upgrade to version 3.0. ®

item.title: Amazon loses first batch of broadband satellites launched on custom rocket
item.description: Amazon’s ambition to operate a constellation of broadband satellites took a hit on Sunday, when 40 of its craft failed to make it into orbit. The failure is significant because it was the first Amazon launch to use a rocket designed especially for the job of carrying its broadband birds to low Earth orbit. The Lockheed/Boeing joint venture United Launch Alliance (ULA) created that rocket, a version of its Vulcan heavy lifter using a six-booster configuration and a Centaur V upper stage optimized to carry payloads into low Earth orbit. Last week, Amazon previewed the launch with a post that noted this mission, code-named LV-01, is the first of 38 planned missions with ULA, and that LV-02 would likely follow within weeks. The two companies planned to test new hardware on the first “several” flights using the custom rocket. Amazon put 40 satellites aboard the Sunday mission and said it is “already planning larger configurations for subsequent missions.” Those plans, and the LV-02 launch, are probably on hold after the rocket suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight. The flight began well, with the Vulcan reaching an altitude of 95 miles (150 km) and completing the first phase of its flight. Six minutes into the mission, the main booster and payload fairing both separated as planned, and ULA lit up the Centaur V’s engines for the first planned firings needed to reach low Earth orbit. Then came the anomaly, which UAL’s live update stream states meant the mission “failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.” “Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something,” UAL wrote. “Since the anomaly just occurred, we don’t have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today.” Amazon already has over 200 satellites in orbit, had hoped to launch its satellite broadband service this year, and plans 20 or more launches in 2027. It is unclear if this mission failure will change those ambitions. ®

item.title: Microsoft lifts Indian cloud prices by 15 percent, cuts costs in China
item.description: Microsoft has announced massive price rises for commercial cloud services in India and New Zealand, but a substantial reduction in China. The software giant sells its cloudy services in many local currencies, at an equivalent rate to the prices it charges in the USA. As exchange rates shift, so do the prices Microsoft charges around the world. Microsoft last week announced the new charges that will come into effect from January 1, 2027, and the news isn’t pleasant for customers in India, who face an increase of 15.7 percent for cloud services and up to 20 percent for some on-prem offerings. New Zealand customers face a ten percent price hike. Customers in China, where Microsoft relies on a local partner called 21Vianet to deliver its cloud, will see costs fall by up to 8.5 percent. Australian buyers will see costs fall by 4.5 percent. The only nation not in Asia on Microsoft’s list is Norway, where prices will ease 5.9 percent. Sega Japan hits double trouble Sega has just had a rotten week that saw it battle a data leak and an outage. The outage impacted the company’s ALL.Net and Aime services, which connect arcade games across different locations. The services include administrative features for arcade operators, plus services for gamers including pre-payment to play, high score and profile recording, and networked gaming. Sega suspended some ALL.Net and Aime services on November 1 after discovering unauthorized access to servers. At least thirteen games and services were then unavailable until around November 15. The company hasn’t explained what went wrong, but assured customers the incident was not a data breach and that payment information was safe. But data did leak for those who subscribe to some Sega newsletters. Sega uses a third-party outfit called Arara Co. to send some emails, and it leaked email addresses. No other personal data leaked from Arara. Sega has nonetheless warned newsletter recipients to watch out for suspicious messages. Alibaba floats chip unit Chinese tech giant Alibaba last week announced its intention to float its T-Head chip design biz on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. The filing announcing the spinoff describes T-Head as “a leading provider of full-stack data center chips which enable system-level compute solutions in China,” suggesting Alibaba doesn’t think buyers in the rest of the world are keen to acquire its chips. T-Head going public “allows a more efficient deployment of Alibaba Group’s financial resources,” the filing states, and should also mean the chip design outfit can more easily find third-party customers. item.content:encoded: Microsoft has announced massive price rises for commercial cloud services in India and New Zealand, but a substantial reduction in China. The software giant sells its cloudy services in many local currencies, at an equivalent rate to the prices it charges in the USA. As exchange rates shift, so do the prices Microsoft charges around the world. Microsoft last week announced the new charges that will come into effect from January 1, 2027, and the news isn’t pleasant for customers in India, who face an increase of 15.7 percent for cloud services and up to 20 percent for some on-prem offerings. New Zealand customers face a ten percent price hike. Customers in China, where Microsoft relies on a local partner called 21Vianet to deliver its cloud, will see costs fall by up to 8.5 percent. Australian buyers will see costs fall by 4.5 percent. The only nation not in Asia on Microsoft’s list is Norway, where prices will ease 5.9 percent. Sega Japan hits double trouble Sega has just had a rotten week that saw it battle a data leak and an outage. The outage impacted the company’s ALL.Net and Aime services, which connect arcade games across different locations. The services include administrative features for arcade operators, plus services for gamers including pre-payment to play, high score and profile recording, and networked gaming. Sega suspended some ALL.Net and Aime services on November 1 after discovering unauthorized access to servers. At least thirteen games and services were then unavailable until around November 15. The company hasn’t explained what went wrong, but assured customers the incident was not a data breach and that payment information was safe. But data did leak for those who subscribe to some Sega newsletters. Sega uses a third-party outfit called Arara Co. to send some emails, and it leaked email addresses. No other personal data leaked from Arara. Sega has nonetheless warned newsletter recipients to watch out for suspicious messages. Alibaba floats chip unit Chinese tech giant Alibaba last week announced its intention to float its T-Head chip design biz on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange. The filing announcing the spinoff describes T-Head as “a leading provider of full-stack data center chips which enable system-level compute solutions in China,” suggesting Alibaba doesn’t think buyers in the rest of the world are keen to acquire its chips. T-Head going public “allows a more efficient deployment of Alibaba Group’s financial resources,” the filing states, and should also mean the chip design outfit can more easily find third-party customers. India bans export of dead batteries The government of India last week banned the export of “Lithium-Ion battery Black Mass” – a powdery substance created during the process of recycling batteries. “It contains recoverable quantities of critical minerals, including lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese,” according to the government’s announcement of the ban, which argues the measure “will increase domestic recovery of lithium, cobalt, nickel and other critical minerals, thereby reducing import dependence and the associated foreign exchange outgo. It will also strengthen supply chains for battery manufacturing, electric vehicles, energy storage and clean-energy technologies.” “Further, the measure will advance the circular economy and ‘urban mining’, reducing reliance on primary mining, while supporting environmentally sound recycling of this hazardous material within the country in accordance with applicable environmental regulations.” Japanese giants to investigate orbiting datacenters Five giant Japanese companies – NTT, Mitsubishi Electric, MUFG Bank, the Development Bank of Japan, and telco NTT DOCOMO – last week signed a memorandum of understanding that will see them jointly explore development and operation of a mega-constellation of satellites. The five “will examine the technical and business feasibility of commercializing a diverse range of services enabled by mega-constellations, including communications, Earth observation, satellite-based positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT), and space data centers.” Mitsubishi already works with the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) to jointly develop and manufacture rockets. The two banks regularly back big infrastructure projects, while the two NTT entities have advanced comms expertise. The five companies didn’t set a deadline for delivery of a plan. If they do decide there’s a business opportunity, they’ll likely need to look beyond Japan for launch capacity as JAXA does not currently possess a re-usable launch vehicle and operates at a modest launch cadence compared to private launch operators. ®

item.title: Vulcan rocket fails during launch, dealing major blow to SpaceX competitors
item.description: United Launch Alliance's Vulcan rocket and 40 Amazon Leo broadband satellites fell back to Earth minutes after liftoff Sunday, a crushing setback that will ripple across all sectors of the US space industry. The Vulcan rocket is on contract to launch roughly half of the US military's national security space missions in the next few years, and Sunday's mission was the first of 38 Vulcan launches booked by Amazon to build out its network of broadband Internet satellites aimed at competing with SpaceX's Starlink. Sunday's failure is expected to ground the rocket for an indefinite period of time. Vulcan is no stranger to close calls, having overcome failures with its strap-on solid rocket boosters on two of its four previous flights. In each case, the rocket corrected for those problems and continued into orbit to deploy its payloads. The incidents trigged months-long reviews and investigations before ULA could resume Vulcan flights. Read full article Comments

item.title: Fanttik’s S1 Pro electric screwdriver is $40 off in the run-up to Black Friday
item.description: Amazon’s early Black Friday promos are already underway , and we’ll be highlighting some of our favorites over the next few days on our Shopping page . Among them is the Fanttik S1 Pro Cordless Electric Screwdriver , which is currently matching its all-time low of $39.99 ($40 off) at Amazon for a limited time. Fanttik S1 Pro Cordless Electric Screwdriver Where to Buy: $79.99 $39.99 at Amazon $79.99 $45.99 at Fanttik Fanttik’s rechargeable tool is designed to make everyday household repairs and DIY projects easier, and it does a good job. Verge commerce editor Brandon Widder once called it his go-to electric screwdriver, noting he’s used it to assemble a bed, tighten bike seats, and perform other small- to medium-sized tasks around the house. It offers three adjustable torque settings, so you can use a gentler setting for more delicate jobs like electronics and more power for tougher projects. Beyond being a capable electric screwdriver, the Fanttik also comes equipped with a few extra conveniences. For example, it features a built-in LED light to help you see screws in darker spaces, such as under a desk or inside a cabinet. The screwdriver also comes with 16 S2 hardened steel bits, including flathead and Torx bits, all of which fit inside an included magnetic storage case. The rechargeable 2,000mAh battery should handle up to 340 screws on a single charge, too, and it supports USB-C so you can quickly charge it between projects.

Verge commerce editor Brandon Widder once called it his go-to electric screwdriver, noting he’s used it to assemble a bed, tighten bike seats, and perform other small- to medium-sized tasks around the house. It offers three adjustable torque settings, so you can use a gentler setting for more delicate jobs like electronics and more power for tougher projects. Beyond being a capable electric screwdriver, the Fanttik also comes equipped with a few extra conveniences. For example, it features a built-in LED light to help you see screws in darker spaces, such as under a desk or inside a cabinet. The screwdriver also comes with 16 S2 hardened steel bits, including flathead and Torx bits, all of which fit inside an included magnetic storage case. The rechargeable 2,000mAh battery should handle up to 340 screws on a single charge, too, and it supports USB-C so you can quickly charge it between projects.

item.title: ‘Grand Theft Auto Flu’: is the whole world really taking the day off work to play GTA VI?
item.description: Headlines have claimed the release of the first new GTA game in 13 years will hugely affect the global economy on Thursday – but there’s another story that’s been left behind A new pandemic is threatening planet Earth. It’s scheduled to hit 19 November. Entire offices and worksites will be emptied; employees struck down by a mysterious illness. But you need not panic: it isn’t fatal. It should pass in a few days. The anticipation for Grand Theft Auto VI, the first new game in the franchise in 13 years, is so high that a steady stream of news coverage has suggested it heralds economic catastrophe due to workers taking time off to play the game. The term “GTA Flu” was coined for the swathe of sickies that reportedly happened when GTA V was released in 2013, and – supposedly – are set to happen again when GTA VI comes out this week. Continue reading...

item.title: LG’s budget-friendly B6E OLED TV is up to 50 percent off this weekend
item.description: LG’s B6E was already one of the most affordable OLED TVs you could buy, but it’s an even better deal now that it’s included as part of Best Buy’s latest doorbuster event. Now through the end of today, November 15th, the 55-inch model is 50 percent off, dropping it to an all-time low of $699.99 ($700 off) at Best Buy . If you want a larger 4K set, the 65- and 77-inch models are also discounted, dropping them to $999.99 ($900 off) and $1,499.99 ($1,200 off) , respectively. LG B6E OLED TV Where to Buy: $1399.99 $699.99 at Best Buy (55-inch) $1899.99 $999.99 at Best Buy (65-inch) $2699.99 $1499.99 at Best Buy (77-inch) Although it’s not as bright as LG’s pricier C6 , the B6E still delivers the excellent contrast and deep blacks OLEDs are often praised for. It’s nearly identical to the standard B6, except it comes with a simpler remote that lacks the motion controls and voice features found on LG’s Magic Remote. It supports Dolby Vision and HDR10 for more lifelike colors and detail in bright and dark scenes, along with Dolby Atmos for more immersive audio. And with Apple AirPlay and Google Cast built in, you can easily stream content from your phone or tablet and access a variety of streaming apps, including Netflix, HBO Max, and YouTube via LG’s webOS platform. The B6 also offers a lot of features gamers will appreciate. It has a 120Hz refresh rate for modern gaming consoles, which is still plenty fast even if it doesn’t rival the 165Hz refresh rate on the C6. It also offers variable refresh rate support — including Nvidia G-Sync and AMD FreeSync Premium — to help minimize screen tearing. You also get a zippy Alpha 8 Gen 3 AI processor and four HDMI 2.1 ports, making it easy to connect multiple consoles. It may lack some of the more advanced features found on LG’s more premium OLED TVs, but at 50 percent off, the B6 is a great option if you want the benefits of OLED without spending a fortune.

item.title: How the world’s fires changed while humanity hit pause
item.description: Wildfires occur worldwide, and they can sometimes become serious threats to people's lives. A series of massive bushfires from 2019 to 2020 swept across southeastern Australia and destroyed thousands of homes. Recently, the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires spread widely across the city, resulting in massive damage to local communities. Many things can cause wildfires, but humans are the only factor that can also make preventative efforts. Measuring people's impact on fire is difficult because of the mix of human and natural influences. A team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recently published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing the COVID-19 era with other years. Data from the 2020 lockdowns suggest that lower human activity at this time had the net effect of lowering average fire activity. Read full article Comments

item.title: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
item.description: The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat. The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. It is a neon-soaked metropolis of sleaze and struggle, hard-partying excess juxtaposed with a barely concealed criminal underworld and unpredictable Florida madness. Continue reading...

item.title: LEO gets a birthday bash, 75 years after clocking in
item.description: Business computing turns 75 this month, and Cambridge's Centre for Computing History is throwing a party for LEO, the machine that helped start it all. The LEO@75 event takes place on Saturday, November 28, from 10am to 5pm, with film screenings, historical displays, and hands-on activities for children. The Register has written about the Centre for Computing History a few times. It's an interactive computer museum just off Coldhams Lane in Cambridge, and back in 2018 it won National Lottery funding to help it "preserve, archive and digitise a range of LEO Computers artefacts, documents and personal memories." Admission supports the museum charity, with student and concession tickets at £10 and family tickets starting at £15. As well as stuff for the grown-ups, including a film screening, it will include events for smaller children (5-7) and a Python coding event for older (12-16) kids. Regular readers might recall our story about the Lyons Electronic Office back in 2021, celebrating its 70th anniversary. The Reg also published an obituary for Mary Coombs, the first female commercial programmer the following year. Coombs started programming LEO in 1952. Both stories offer more on the machine and the people behind it. LEO was an early computer, but from three-quarters of a century away, it's easy to miss just how early. Its design was based on Cambridge University's EDSAC, developed by a team led by the late, great Sir Maurice Wilkes. The Reg mentioned EDSAC in our obituary for Wilkes, and went into more detail for his centenary in 2013 . It also crops up in our Geek's Guide to Cambridge . The design of EDSAC was directly inspired by John von Neumann's famous, and incomplete, "First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC" – which The Reg talked about in 2011 . The draft report was circulated in 1945, based on the proposal for EDVAC, four years before the hardware was delivered. That was also the year John Mauchly and J. Presper Eckert completed its predecessor, ENIAC. In its original form, ENIAC was programmed by setting switches and reconnecting cables; EDVAC, by contrast, was designed to store its instructions in memory. The report set out what's now called the "von Neumann architecture." Wilkes and Douglas Hartree drew on those ideas in developing EDSAC, LEO's immediate forerunner and one of the world's earliest practical stored-program computers. The first working electronic stored-program machine was the Manchester "Baby," the Small-Scale Experimental Machine, which ran its first program in 1948 . EDSAC ran its first program in May 1949 – a few months before the delivery of BINAC, Eckert and Mauchly's first stored-program machine. LEO ran its first commercial application in 1951. That was also the year the US Census Bureau took delivery of Eckert and Mauchly's UNIVAC I . ®

item.description: Fears for national college entrance exam next week as test taker admits sending photos of questions to AI tool The marks attained by the top scorer ⁠on South Korea’s national exam for aspiring tax accountants this year seemed too good to be true. On Sunday, sceptics were ⁠proven right when he ⁠confessed to ​using generative AI to cheat. The scandal has followed months of speculation after he scored near-perfect marks on hundreds of questions over two exams ⁠taken in April and July. It has also raised the stakes for organisers of South Korea’s annual college entrance exam this Thursday. Continue reading...

When you visit the site of one you’ve heard good things about you are asked to verify that you are human. Instead of clicking on a series of images, or typing letters that appear, just as you have seen before, you are asked to press a series of keys and then press enter. Continue reading...

item.title: ‘Jensen Huang lost his mind’: how AI’s smartest man fell for the world’s oldest trick
item.description: Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected spy is Silicon Valley’s worst nightmare come true The resignation this week of Nvidia’s founder and CEO Jensen Huang is one of the most astonishing corporate scandals in memory, featuring allegations of international espionage and extramarital affairs involving one of the world’s most powerful men. As investigations mount into what went wrong at the $4tn chip company, the saga may also become a milestone in the decades-long history of spies infiltrating the US tech industry. Huang admitted to being unfaithful to his wife of 41 years in a letter to employees this past weekend, following a report from the New York Times that the tech mogul had a close relationship with a woman US officials suspect of spying for China’s government. Huang resigned on Thursday after 33 years as CEO amid reports of two additional affairs with Nvidia employees, causing the world’s most valuable chip company’s stock to plummet. Continue reading...

item.title: SpaceX returned its Starship rocket on Saturday—but there's a catch
item.description: STARBASE, Texas —The black and silver ship fell out of the sky, emerging from the cloud deck near the very end of its flight. Incongruously, the rocket flew horizontal until the last moment when three Raptor rocket engines ignited and it swooped into a vertical position. Slowly, gently, haltingly, the Starship upper stage eased its way toward the waiting tower where two arms extended outward, awaiting expectantly. The margins are so incredibly narrow. Two nubs on either side of the rocket, each protruding only about one foot, were the only purchase the rocket would have on the arms. Then, less than a minute after it came into view, the Starship upper stage was snagged by the launch tower, as snug as you like. And so it was all over. SpaceX, nearly a quarter of a century after its founding, had just taken a hugely significant step toward developing and optimizing a massive, rapidly reusable rocket. Read full article Comments

item.title: Art ‘must not be sacrificed on the altar of corporate profit’, Liberal senator says as AI policy debate rages
item.description: Andrew McLachlan says he chooses ‘real forests over virtual ones’ as he urges Labor government to consider AI’s impact on artists and environment Get our daily political email , free app or daily news podcast The outspoken Liberal senator Andrew McLachlan has raised the alarm about the approach of his party and the Labor government to AI, saying artists’ copyright must not be “sacrificed” for investment and building new datacentres must not be prioritised above environmental concerns. As Labor considers copyright changes in an AI policy suite including datacentres, online safety, energy resources and economic benefits, the South Australian backbencher added weight to mooted constitutional challenges as to whether watering down copyright law would be an illegal acquisition of property . But finding an item that elicits a squeal of delight from its recipient is one of the best parts of this time of year, when you have a little help. Our seasoned writers and shopping experts got into the holiday spirit early, vetting gifts across kitchen, home, tech and 10 more categories. item.title: James Webb telescope finds ice older than the star it orbits
item.description: Beta Pictoris is a young star, roughly 20 million years old, and located about 64 light-years away from Earth. It is surrounded by a vast disk of dust and rubble where planets are still forming—astronomers have already found three. In a new Science study, a team led by Sarah Betti, an astronomer at the Space Telescope Science Institute in Baltimore, used the James Webb Space Telescope to look for ice in this disk. Researchers found both water and carbon dioxide ice. The water ice is glassy rather than crystalline, and it is mixed with carbon dioxide in roughly the same proportions we see in comets of our own Solar System. This suggests ingredients necessary to form water-rich worlds might be common around young stars. The missing ice Beta Pictoris is one of the best studied stars in the sky. Its disk was among the first ever imaged, back in 1984, and we see it almost exactly edge-on, which makes it a natural laboratory for studying how planetary systems grow. It's what astronomers call a debris disk, where the dust is constantly replenished by collisions among comets and planetesimals, small bodies that are the building blocks of planets. Read full article Comments

item.title: Winemakers are learning that conservation can be good for business
item.description: More than 500 vineyards are scattered across the slopes and valleys of South Africa’s Western Cape , one of the world’s most biologically diverse landscapes. The region produces about 90 percent of South Africa’s wine , but winemakers there are increasingly struggling with drought, excessive heat and erratic rainfall. Temperatures in the region have risen 1.5 to 2 times faster than the global average over the past five decades. And extreme storms have become more intense as climate variability increases. The late 2010s brought a significant challenge for winemakers, as three years of severe drought placed vineyards under intense stress and reduced grape production. As climate variability places increasing pressure on grape production, many wine producers are building on sustainability measures that have long been part of vineyard management. Read full article Comments

item.title: Microsoft's school email bill gives rivals something to smile about
item.description: The fallout from Microsoft's education price rises and service cuts continues as institutions weigh the prospect of bigger bills, and the Windows maker's rivals struggle not to pull "I told you so" faces. The main takeaways are that free student email and collaboration services are being retired, and storage entitlements are changing. These changes generally apply at institutions' first renewal or extension on or after January 1, 2028. Microsoft announced the new plans last week, and the UK's Department for Education described itself as "disappointed" at the news. As well it might be, although the UK government has rarely seen a deal from Microsoft that it didn't like . Or, for that matter, other US tech giants . Exactly how much educational institutions will have to spend remains unclear. Mary Jo Foley of Directions on Microsoft put indicative student pricing at $2 per year for Microsoft 365 Education A2, $4 for A3, and $6 for A5, with Teams adding another dollar annually. Faculty licenses cost considerably more, while the new A7 student tier jumps to $385 a year before Teams. Foley cautioned that these were approximate figures, with actual prices set by Microsoft's partners. The new no-cost student tier, Microsoft 365 Education A0, is a poor replacement for Office 365 A1: it excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also requires full paid faculty coverage on A2 or higher and students who actively use Windows devices for education – potentially awkward for institutions running fleets of Chromebooks. A few dollars per student might not sound alarming. Multiply that across an institution, however, and something that used to be free becomes a recurring bill. Michael Meeks, CEO of Collabora Productivity, told The Register: "Free was the bait on the hook, and Microsoft spent years reeling in schools' email accounts, documents, identity management and classrooms onto its cloud." A poster on the edugeek.net forums commented: "This was always going to happen, I remember thinking this when we moved over to the MS free cloud solution. It will be free until they decide it isn't." The risk for Microsoft is that there are options. Meeks told us: "Schools now have a year to plan, and, in our experience with other large-scale educational projects, such as the University of Lille, that can be enough time to migrate properly." Other options include Nextcloud, which will be rolled out as part of Germany's Educational Cloud Infrastructure . Several Swiss universities also migrated to the service over an August weekend. According to Nextcloud, 39,500 students, teachers, and researchers, along with 585 terabytes of data, were shifted. Both Nextcloud and Collabora Productivity also highlight another factor that could drive educational institutions away from Microsoft: sovereignty. item.content:encoded: The fallout from Microsoft's education price rises and service cuts continues as institutions weigh the prospect of bigger bills, and the Windows maker's rivals struggle not to pull "I told you so" faces. The main takeaways are that free student email and collaboration services are being retired, and storage entitlements are changing. Microsoft announced the new plans last week, and the UK's Department for Education described itself as "disappointed" at the news. As well it might be, although the UK government has rarely seen a deal from Microsoft that it didn't like . Or, for that matter, other US tech giants . Exactly how much educational institutions will have to spend remains unclear. Mary Jo Foley of Directions on Microsoft put indicative student pricing at $2 per year for Microsoft 365 Education A2, $4 for A3, and $6 for A5, with Teams adding another dollar annually. Faculty licenses cost considerably more, while the new A7 student tier jumps to $385 a year before Teams. Foley cautioned that these were approximate figures, with actual prices set by Microsoft's partners. The new no-cost student tier, Microsoft 365 Education A0, is a poor replacement for Office 365 A1: it excludes Exchange Online, SharePoint Online, and Teams. Eligibility also requires full paid faculty coverage on A2 or higher and students who actively use Windows devices for education – potentially awkward for institutions running fleets of Chromebooks. A few dollars per student might not sound alarming. Multiply that across an institution, however, and something that used to be free becomes a recurring bill. Michael Meeks, CEO of Collabora Productivity, told The Register: "Free was the bait on the hook, and Microsoft spent years reeling in schools' email accounts, documents, identity management and classrooms onto its cloud." A poster on the edugeek.net forums commented: "This was always going to happen, I remember thinking this when we moved over to the MS free cloud solution. It will be free until they decide it isn't." The risk for Microsoft is that there are options. Meeks told us: "Schools now have a year to plan, and, in our experience with other large-scale educational projects, such as the University of Lille, that can be enough time to migrate properly." Other options include Nextcloud, which will be rolled out as part of Germany's Educational Cloud Infrastructure . Several Swiss universities also migrated to the service over an August weekend. According to Nextcloud, 39,500 students, teachers, and researchers, along with 585 terabytes of data, were shifted. Both Nextcloud and Collabora Productivity also highlight another factor that could drive educational institutions away from Microsoft: sovereignty. Dr Patrick Alberts, managing director of messaging provider Element, told The Register : "When an organization is locked to a vendor, it should be no surprise when that vendor takes advantage. When switching is made difficult, the vendor holds all the leverage. They can raise prices or slash services on a whim, knowing customers will swallow the pain rather than rip out the infrastructure. "Yet it's a bold move, given European governments are proactively following a digitally sovereign strategy." Switching suppliers still takes planning, and the alternatives won't necessarily replace every Microsoft service. But the Windows behemoth has given educational institutions a fresh reason to investigate – and its rivals a particularly convenient opening pitch. ®

item.title: Big Tech takes a beating as online safety experts accuse companies of doing bare minimum
item.description: Technology companies are doing just enough to show a degree of compliance with the UK's Online Safety Act, but are failing to meet the needs of the individuals and young victims the legislation exists to protect, experts say. A panel of online safety pros assembled before Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee on Tuesday, taking aim at the likes of Google, Microsoft, Meta, and ByteDance for failing to act on important matters. Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University and expert on violence against women and girls (VAWG), was especially critical of major search engine providers for their inconsistent downranking of harmful content search terms. "Rape porn," for example, is correctly downranked and no user sees any relevant links until the tenth page of results, although adjacent terms such as "unwilling porn" can be found as early as the third page, McGlynn said. "I just think if someone spent a little more time thinking 'I really want to minimize the risk of this material appearing,' I would take a systematic approach," she told the committee. "I would downrank 'unwilling' and 'unwanted,' and I would downrank 'asleep porn' as well… because it just means that it's easily findable. "So, they don't rank some of them, but just not systematically or wholly consistently." McGlynn went on to say that during her own research, "force porn" was rightly downranked heavily, although terms as similar as "forced porn" were not. "If you were trying to think of the words that would be similar to say rape, and rape porn is extreme porn and it's not supposed to be on those platforms anymore, you would think of words like unwilling and unwanted," she added. "And we know your algorithm would." Google inevitably took much of McGlynn's flak due to its dominance of the search engine market, although the professor said the same issues can be observed on Bing, too. Alexandra Whiston-Dew, partner at law firm Miscon de Raya, argued that search engines have such an important role in regulating the OSA, noting the limited resources at Ofcom's disposal. She said that more needs to be done from the tech side to ensure different parties in the chain of publication are detected early and downranked or blocked accordingly. There are publications, for example, that actively advertise themselves as websites that host illegal content, and these appear to be missing from the search engines' crosshairs. "So, they are spotlighting the fact that they are publishing illegal content, and this is going under the radar not only from the search engines but also the other platforms and the businesses in the chain of publication," said Whiston-Dew. "Also Ofcom needs to really pull all of their resources together and attack that receptacle of illegal content." Similarly, McGlynn raised the issue of porn sites continuing to host extreme porn, as they are legally allowed to do, to make it available to less regulated territories. item.dc:creator: Connor Jones
item.content:encoded: Technology companies are doing just enough to show a degree of compliance with the UK's Online Safety Act, but are failing to meet the needs of the individuals and young victims the legislation exists to protect, experts say. A panel of online safety pros assembled before Parliament's Communications and Digital Committee on Tuesday, taking aim at the likes of Google, Microsoft, Meta, and ByteDance for failing to act on important matters. Clare McGlynn, professor of law at Durham University and expert on violence against women and girls (VAWG), was especially critical of major search engine providers for their inconsistent downranking of harmful content search terms. "Rape porn," for example, is correctly downranked and no user sees any relevant links until the tenth page of results, although adjacent terms such as "unwilling porn" can be found as early as the third page, McGlynn said. "I just think if someone spent a little more time thinking 'I really want to minimize the risk of this material appearing,' I would take a systematic approach," she told the committee. "I would downrank 'unwilling' and 'unwanted,' and I would downrank 'asleep porn' as well… because it just means that it's easily findable. "So, they don't rank some of them, but just not systematically or wholly consistently." McGlynn went on to say that during her own research, "force porn" was rightly downranked heavily, although terms as similar as "forced porn" were not. "If you were trying to think of the words that would be similar to say rape, and rape porn is extreme porn and it's not supposed to be on those platforms anymore, you would think of words like unwilling and unwanted," she added. "And we know your algorithm would." Google inevitably took much of McGlynn's flak due to its dominance of the search engine market, although the professor said the same issues can be observed on Bing, too. Alexandra Whiston-Dew, partner at law firm Miscon de Raya, argued that search engines have such an important role in regulating the OSA, noting the limited resources at Ofcom's disposal. She said that more needs to be done from the tech side to ensure different parties in the chain of publication are detected early and downranked or blocked accordingly. There are publications, for example, that actively advertise themselves as websites that host illegal content, and these appear to be missing from the search engines' crosshairs. "So, they are spotlighting the fact that they are publishing illegal content, and this is going under the radar not only from the search engines but also the other platforms and the businesses in the chain of publication," said Whiston-Dew. "Also Ofcom needs to really pull all of their resources together and attack that receptacle of illegal content." Similarly, McGlynn raised the issue of porn sites continuing to host extreme porn, as they are legally allowed to do, to make it available to less regulated territories. With the harmful content still on the site, all it takes is a VPN connection to access it, and bypass the age assurance mechanisms in the process. Success of user reports trails away As well as a piecemeal approach to downranking extreme content, experts said that tech platforms initially showed a strong appetite in quickly handling content-takedown requests, although this appears to have waned substantially. Citing data from domestic violence and VAWG charity Refuge [PDF], Janaya Walker, interim director at the End Violence Against Women Coalition (EVAW), said that before November 2025, the success rate for these kinds of reports made using Refuge’s Trusted Flagger team stood at 53.7 percent. Over the past 12 months, however, this dropped to just 18.2 percent. Further, since November 2025, zero percent of reports made to Meta have been successful, according to Refuge’s figures. The charity’s Trusted Flagger team works closely with social media platforms to report content that victims may have reported to it. The idea is that if the report comes from an authority like Refuge, it is acted upon more quickly. Walker said there was real concern about how platforms behave and whether they comply with existing regulation, and about what that means for specialist services supporting survivors in limbo, particularly without an online commission to advocate for victims' and survivors' interests. Meta did not immediately respond to questions about its takedown rate, but according to its Community Standards Enforcement Report , it removed 27.8 million posts related to adult nudity and sexual activity between April and June 2026. The report does not include a category devoted to VAWG-related reports, so take the data with the appropriate level of scrutiny. Neither Google, Microsoft, nor TikTok responded to requests for comment. The findings from Refuge and the discussion in Parliament this week reflect the wider concern about the efficacy of the OSA, and how online safety experts are frustrated with how little impact it has had, more than a year after the new duties came into force. England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, told the same committee in September that the OSA "has made absolutely no difference " to children's access to harmful content online, as evidenced by the accounts of young people themselves. Amid discussions from the panel of experts this week regarding the need for a civil redress scheme, McGlynn pointed to British Columbia's system as an example of how other countries are going further to protect people from online harms. She said: "...an individual still does not have the right to demand an image be taken down. And that is where I think we just lack that capacity to say to an individual, 'this is what you need to do, and you can bring this legal action, for example, against X, against the perpetrator, you can get the material deleted.' "In British Columbia in Canada, they have a swift online civil redress system where you can make these claims, and you can get instant orders to get this material taken down, and you can even get compensation for some of the harm suffered. "So other countries are doing more, if you like, to give the individuals that right as well as all the other measures at the platform level." ®

item.title: Starship flight 15 powers to orbit—setting up a possible catch on Saturday
item.description: STARBASE, Texas—Starship lifted off right on schedule Friday from South Texas, making its 15th test flight in more than three years. The largely successful launch took place in the early evening; as the massive rocket rose into the atmosphere, the Sun sank toward the western horizon. Conditions were ideal for the launch, with the atmospheric winds so calm the rocket’s white plume did not dissipate for many minutes. The weather in South Texas is not always comfortable; summers are long and hot. Friday evening was perfect at Starbase. The first stage ascended toward space flawlessly, releasing the upper stage above the Gulf of Mexico. From there, the Starship upper stage ignited its Raptor engines and powered its way into a nominal orbit. This was the second time SpaceX has flown Starship into low-Earth orbit. Read full article Comments

item.title: FAA has lifted its third-ever nationwide ground stop
item.description: The Federal Administration lifted its third-ever nationwide ground stop after several hours Friday evening. Domestic flights were cleared to begin taking off at 8:35 pm EST. FAA Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy cautioned that, barring massive system updates, there will be "more of these" ahead. "Today's nationwide ground stop happened because our air traffic control system is operating on DECADES-OLD analog equipment that simply cannot compete with the demands of the 21st century," Duffy posted on X . Over a million travelers have been affected by the delays, with some airlines cancelling flights for the remainder of Friday. "Due to the ongoing ground stop, Air Canada has cancelled all flights to and from the United States for the remainder of the evening," the airline said . Read full article Comments

item.title: FAA blames ground stop on faulty copper wiring
item.description: The US Federal Aviation Administration on Friday issued an advisory that prevented the takeoff of flights in US airspace for around five hours, creating chaos for travelers and airports. The stop was finally lifted around 8:30 PM Eastern Time, but only after thousands of flights were canceled or delayed, leaving travelers stranded. In a press conference Saturday, Transportation Secretary Duffy attributed the FAA ground stop to problems with copper wiring during an L3Harris network upgrade. Duffy said it has yet to be determined whether the issue was incompetence or a faulty router. In a statement provided to The Register on Saturday, a spokesperson for L3Harris said, “L3Harris has been modernizing the communications infrastructure supporting the National Airspace System in close coordination with the FAA. With safety and reliability as our highest priorities, L3Harris, together with its telco partners and the FAA, has completed more than 70 percent of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber optic system. We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation’s air travel. L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.” The stop was issued on Friday around the middle of the day ET. "The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," said US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy in a statement on Friday. "FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them." A spokesperson at the FAA press office reached by phone at the time said he was unable to provide further information. And an email response from the agency repeated Duffy's statement. The FAA ATCSCC advisory halted departing flights and said international flights would be dealt with individually. The notice said, "Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety. Attention all aircraft operators, by order of the Federal Aviation Command Center all airports are ground stopped. All departing traffic should remain stopped until further notice. Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis." Doug Yakel, public information officer for San Francisco International Airport, said, "FAA confirms nationwide ground stop, other reporting indicates a communications issue between Air Route Traffic Control Centers (ARTCCs). Aircraft already enroute to SFO still landing here but departing aircraft not taking off right now." An update issued at 2:02 pm PT described the problem as "a temporary telecommunications outage." The FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure (FTI) is managed by L3Harris. The network provides secure communication between more than 4,400 facilities. ® Updated at 0039 UTC Sunday UTC with the administration's explanation for the stop. Updated at 0

item.title: Millions of Americans are not taking their GLP-1 drugs as prescribed
item.description: GLP-1 medications are everywhere these days. The peptide-based drugs are both highly effective and wildly popular for diabetes, weight loss and a growing range of connected chronic health conditions, including cardiovascular disease and obstructive sleep apnea. But, amid the boom, the latest data suggests millions of Americans have turned to unapproved versions and are using the potent drugs in ways doctors never intended, raising questions about what that real-world use means for safety and efficacy. In a study published this week , researchers at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention broke down survey data of GLP-1 use collected between July and August of 2025. Based on responses from over 8,000 US adults, the researchers estimate that about one in 10 US adults (9.8 percent) used a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, aka GLP-1 medication, in 2025. That's around 27 million adults. The study was published in the CDC's Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. Among GLP-1 users, nearly half (44 percent) reported using their GLP-1 in a way that was different from how it was prescribed. Users skipped doses, delayed getting refills, and used smaller doses than prescribed, among other changes. More than half of the people modifying how they used the drug said the changes were because of cost or availability reasons. Cost and access barriers were most pronounced among younger GLP-1 users. Fifty-eight percent of adults 14­–39 years old who modified their use cited cost as a barrier, compared with just 20 percent of adults 65 or older who said the same. Read full article Comments

item.title: FAA expands AI advice to manage air traffic congestion across entire US airspace
item.description: The US government has expanded the use of an AI tool for advising air traffic controllers to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system. Airline executives have voiced support for the rollout, but the US labor union representing air traffic controllers has said it was not involved in designing or testing the AI-driven system. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment. “After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10. Read full article Comments

item.title: Chinese AI labs are training models on Nvidia's Blackwell despite export controls, says ex-OpenAI engineer
item.description: US export controls are not stopping AI labs in China from using restricted Nvidia chips, according to a report from a former OpenAI engineer. Will DePue, who left the AI giant earlier this year to launch Unemployment Labs, an AI research consultancy, published forensic evidence showing that "DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group have gained access to Nvidia's Blackwell GPUs, despite restrictions on exporting these chips to China, and are using that hardware to create their AI models." "This sounds insane, but I discovered that almost every AI model carries a hidden signature of the GPU that trained it," said DePue in a social media post . "When a model is first set up, the starting values of its weights are laid out in a pattern that depends on the exact GPU. Each combination of GPU and seed number produces a unique pattern – a sort of fingerprint of the hardware used to create the model. Traces of that pattern survive training into the published model." It doesn't sound that insane. The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang followed from revelations that he had an affair with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who, in 2023, founded Singapore-based Megaspeed International. That company is reportedly under investigation by US authorities for allegedly smuggling Nvidia chips to China. Huang's departure coincides with a renewed push to tighten US chip export controls. House Speaker Mike Johnson supports the idea . And there are at least four bills awaiting consideration that aim to limit China's access to leading edge AI tech: the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act, Match Act, and the Cloud Security Act. On Monday, US Senators Jim Banks (R-Ind.) and Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) cited Jensen Huang's "relationship with a suspected Chinese spy" as a justification for passing the AI Overwatch Act, which would codify the Trump administration's existing chip export controls. The Trump administration on Thursday said it's not sure whether Alice Huang was a spy, an allegation denied by Beijing and currently under investigation by the FBI. Whatever the case, the current rules clearly are not working. Only a few weeks ago, Lava, an Israel-based security company, said it had found "32 Nvidia B300 GPUs, part of Nvidia's Blackwell Ultra generation, through publicly exposed monitoring endpoints with IP addresses geolocated to China." These GPUs, Lava noted, are subject to US export controls [PDF]. The security biz said its findings followed from the exposure of monitoring systems intended for internal infrastructure management that were publicly exposed. How DePue reached his conclusion The analysis published through DePue's consultancy, "Top Chinese Frontier AI Models Carry the Fingerprint of Export-Controlled Nvidia Blackwell GPUs," takes a different approach: analyzing the published weights of various models from Chinese AI labs.
